newsitem.title: SIERRA LEONE: Sierra Leone peace march wins little support.
newsitem.headline: Sierra Leone peace march wins little support.

text.p: A demonstration called by Sierra Leone's coupmakers against foreign intervention drew little support on Sunday despite the soldiers' warnings of a military strike on the city.

Knots of supporters of the army rulers chanting "We want peace" and carrying a white banner with "We love AFRC" marched through the city but the crowd was far from the millions called for by the Armed Forces Ruling Council (AFRC).

About 5,000 people turned out at the 50,000-capacity national stadium for a prayer meeting attended by AFRC chairman Major Johnny Paul Koroma. The council's secretary-general, Andrew Koroma, read his speech on his behalf.

"It now only remains for me to appeal to the international community to hear the cry and concern of the nation against this imminent threat of invasion of our country, which will no doubt bring more destruction of life and property to our historic city," Koroma said.
He said the alliance between the RUF and the army had ended the insecurity of six years of rebel war and it was now safe to travel all over the interior.

Nigeria has been building up its troops in Freetown since the coup and is widely expected to stage another military strike after last Monday's unsuccessful attempt to force out the coup leaders and restore civilian president Ahmad Tejan Kabbah.
"If President Kabbah was to come back, through military intervention, he would see a devastated city full of corpses." the AFRC chairman told reporters before the prayer meeting.
State radio said a large quantity of property looted after the May 25 coup had been recovered and invited people to come to military headquarters to retrieve it.
The coup makers have sent envoys to meet West African leaders to explain their takeover and seek their support.
A delegation led by diplomat Daouda Kamara met Ivory Coast's President Henri Konan Bedie, who helped mediate between the civilian government and rebels last year.
Ivorian officials said Sunday's meeting did not constitute recognition of the military government and Bedie had told them his country could not support their action.
The AFRC reopened the country's borders and air and sea ports on Sunday. Director of Defence Information Colonel Abdul Sesay said they wanted trade to resume.
Many of the Lebanese who dominate business have fled. Food prices have soared, and basic imported items like rice, sugar and flour, and kerosene and petrol are in short supply.
The central bank was burned down in the coup, and only the black market is operating. The leone currency has fallen from 860 to the dollar before the coup to 1,300 to the dollar now.
Rebels allied to the coupmakers took control of Hastings airport, which Nigeria had been using to fly in troops and supplies for its nearby military base.
The loss of Hastings, on Freetown's eastern outskirts, leaves the Nigerians reliant on the remote international airport at Lungi, creating logistical problems for any military strike.

Rebel commander Captain Johandes Roberts told journalists who visited Hastings on Sunday that they had seized the airfield on Friday after two helicopters landed carrying ammunition. The Nigerians had assured them they were bringing medical supplies.
He said they had captured two Nigerian officers and were holding them at Benguma military training centre near Hastings.
On Saturday, 50 members of the dissolved 80-seat parliament met in defiance of a ban on political activity to denounce the coup and call for Kabbah's return.
The coupmakers have been meeting civilian politicians trying to win them over and have proposed a government of national unity. So far no one has accepted.
Witnesses said a boat left for Guinea on Saturday carrying more of Kabbah's ministers to join him in exile.
